title: “I’ve seen this before...”
author: Jenny R. Allen
summary: Jenny R. Allen opens with the story of being put on probation as a young newspaper reporter and spending months polishing her writing, only to learn the real problem was that she was a poor reporter. She uses it to argue that when a problem looks familiar, leaders reach for the solution that worked before and so fix the wrong thing. The first plausible explanation reduces uncertainty, and because it invites investment of budget, people and time, it becomes harder to undo if the diagnosis was wrong. She names experience, anchoring and expertise as the forces that lead people to latch on to a single explanation, and illustrates with a sales manager who orders training when the cause may be a competitor, a reporting bug or a restructuring. Her remedy is the simple question, what else could it be, asked before committing to a solution.
points: Familiarity is not the same as correctness: leaders default to what worked before and decorate the wrong solution like a gingerbread house.
Experience, anchoring and expertise combine to make the first plausible explanation feel true and shape the evidence people notice afterwards.
The more a team invests in a diagnosis, the harder it is to reverse, so the time to challenge it is before committing resources.
Asking what else could it be, especially when someone says they have seen this before, surfaces alternative causes before an elegant solution is built.
The question works only where you have the power to persuade, since a senior leader set on a solution may not be moved.
quotes: When you encounter something that seems familiar, you’re likely to handle it in the way you handled it before. Easy peasy. Your previous experience becomes the scaffolding for the solution.

A sales manager sees declining numbers. He thinks back to a customer visit the week before, when one rep wasn’t particularly crisp on the close. He brings in training for a refresher on selling techniques.
The first plausible explanation of a problem gives us something to latch onto. If it’s X, I can do Y… and off you go, charting a path to the solution.
Anchoring. The first explanation becomes the reference point for the thinking that follows. Once you have that working theory, you start noticing the evidence that supports it.
Expertise. The IT guy will see a systems problem. The Six Sigma black belt will see a process problem. The expertise leads the witness - and becomes the lens through which people view the problem.

But acting on it means investing in it - with budget, people, time, or all three. And the more you invest in the diagnosis that drove the solution, the harder it becomes to undo if the diagnosis turns out to be wrong.
But where you do have the power to persuade, asking “What else could it be?” can save you from delivering a really elegant solution to a problem you don’t have.
